question: How can linear decision boundaries and LDA be generalised to overlapping classes and nonlinear boundaries (support vector machines, kernels, FDA, PDA, MDA)?
contributions: Support vector classifier for the nonseparable case via slack variables and cost parameter C
SVM via kernels as loss+penalty (hinge loss) and RKHS function estimation; comparison with logistic regression
Path algorithm for the SVM; SVM regression
Flexible, penalized and mixture discriminant analysis as generalisations of LDA via optimal scoring

limits: Experiments are small simulations (mixture data; skin-of-the-orange; waveform; vowel); no large real data SVM benchmark in the chapter.
In the skin-of-the-orange comparison SVM cost C is tuned on the test error, favouring the SVMs, while BRUTO and MARS smoothing parameters were not tuned on test error (p.431-432).
In Fig 12.3 the regularisation parameter and gamma are likewise chosen to achieve good test error, so the reported test errors are optimistic.
Sample sizes and test set size of the Chapter 2 mixture example are not restated here; no seeds for Fig 12.2, 12.3, 12.5, 12.13.
Table 12.3 neural-network rows come from a neural network archive; training error not given for several rows.
Authors concede the VC bound (12.51) depends on observed feature values (balls around data points), so VC complexity is not fixed a priori (p.438).
Authors concede SVMs do not scale well with N (m^3 + mN + mpN); advice to search the web for latest technology; now dated (2009; software mda, svmpath in R).
Statements such as the SVM performing well in many real problems are as of the time of writing (2009).
practices: Use the proportional-slack constraint y_i f(x_i) >= M(1 - xi_i) (12.6); the absolute version (12.5) is nonconvex (Sec 12.2, p.419).
Choose the cost parameter C by cross-validation; the proportion of support points as a LOO bound is too high to be useful (Sec 12.2.2, p.421).
Common usage sets C high, which often overfits; the best C depends strongly on the radial kernel scale gamma, so tune C and gamma together (Sec 12.3.5, p.432, Fig 12.6).
To fit the SVM over the whole sequence of C values efficiently, use the path algorithm (R package svmpath) rather than refitting (Sec 12.3.5, p.433-434).
Small C gives smoother boundary (small ||beta||); large C discourages any positive xi_i and gives a wiggly overfit boundary (Sec 12.3.1, p.424).
SVM kernels cannot adapt to a relevant subspace; with noise features prefer adaptive methods (BRUTO, MARS) or build the subspace into the kernel (Sec 12.3.4, p.431-432).
Kernel degree matters a lot: a polynomial kernel of the true degree (2) does best, higher degrees do much worse (Sec 12.3.4, p.432).

Do not treat the kernel trick or the avoidance of the curse of dimensionality as unique to SVMs; any convex loss with a squared-norm penalty has the finite-dimensional kernel form (12.28) (Sec 12.3, 12.3.3, p.424, 428).
The kernel shortcut relies on the squared L2 penalty; it does not hold for the L1 norm, which may give a superior model (Sec 12.3.7, p.436).
For regression with epsilon-insensitive loss, scale the response and use preset epsilon and Huber c (c = 1.345), and estimate lambda by cross-validation (Sec 12.3.6, p.435).
For multiclass SVM, build a classifier per pair of classes and choose the class that dominates most, or use a multinomial loss with a kernel (Sec 12.3.8, p.437).
The SVM hinge loss estimates the classifier itself, not class probabilities; use the Huberised square hinge or logistic loss if probabilities are needed (Sec 12.3.2, p.427).

Compute FDA as multiresponse regression on the indicator matrix, eigen-decompose Y^T S Y for optimal scores, then update the fit; with a linear-operator regression this is a single eigen-decomposition (Sec 12.5.1, p.444-445).
In FDA, reduced-rank discriminant subspaces gave the best vowel results (Table 12.3, p.444).
Use PDA with a roughness penalty when predictors are many and strongly correlated (signals, images), to avoid noisy, sign-alternating LDA coefficients (Sec 12.6, p.446-447).
Initialise MDA by k-means with multiple random starts within each class, with user-supplied number of subclasses R_k (Sec 12.7, p.449).
Do not choose C by minimising the SRM bound: it is not clear it beats cross-validation (Sec 12.3.8, p.438).

terms.definition: observations with nonzero alpha_i-hat; beta-hat is represented in terms of them alone
proportional amount by which the prediction f(x_i) is on the wrong side of its margin; misclassification when xi_i > 1
replaces the constant bound on sum xi_i in the primal (12.8); separable case corresponds to C = infinity; equals 1/lambda in the loss+penalty form
K(x,x') = <h(x),h(x')>, computes inner products in the transformed space; should be symmetric positive (semi-)definite
L(y,f) = [1 - yf]_+; population minimizer is sign[Pr(Y=+1|x) - 1/2]
loss for which, if data are separable, the limit of beta-hat_lambda as lambda -> 0 defines the optimal separating hyperplane (Rosset et al. 2004b); all of Table 12.1 except squared error
V_eps(r) = 0 if |r| < eps, |r| - eps otherwise; used by support vector regression
Rosset and Zhu 2007 loss that converts smoothly to a linear loss at yf = -1
LDA recast as linear regression on optimally scored class labels, then the linear fit replaced by nonparametric regression
LDA in an enlarged basis space with a quadratic penalty lambda*Omega, penalized Mahalanobis distance (Sigma_W + lambda Omega)^-1
each class modelled as a mixture of Gaussians with R_k prototypes and a shared covariance Sigma; fitted by EM
choose class scores theta_l and linear maps eta_l minimising average squared residual (12.53) subject to orthogonality and normalisation

code.snippet: min_{beta,beta0} (1/2)||beta||^2 + C sum_i xi_i  subject to xi_i >= 0, y_i(x_i^T beta + beta0) >= 1 - xi_i for all i
min_{beta0,beta} sum_i [1 - y_i f(x_i)]_+ + (lambda/2)||beta||^2, with lambda = 1/C (loss + penalty form)

f-hat(x) = sum_i alpha-hat_i y_i K(x, x_i) + beta0-hat
